Complicate

/KOM-pluh-kayt/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Complicate means to make something more difficult, confusing, or intricate than it was before.

House rules that let players trade cards will complicate an otherwise simple board game.

Worked Example

Halfway through the renovation, the workers uncovered an old gas line that will complicate every remaining step of the project.

The project was already planned out; the buried gas line adds new tangles — permits, rerouting, safety checks — to steps that used to be straightforward. That added difficulty is exactly what it means to complicate something.

Antonyms

simplify

simplify: to make easier or clearer

streamline

streamline: to strip down for smooth efficiency

How Strong Is It? — inconvenience → complicate → confound

inconvenience vs. complicate

inconvenience vs. complicate: To inconvenience someone is to cost them a little time; to complicate their task is to add real tangles to the task itself.

confound vs. complicate

confound vs. complicate: To complicate a problem is to tie new knots in it; to confound someone is to leave them unable to see a way through at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — com-

Prefix — com-: together, with (Latin)

Root — plic

Root — plic: to fold (Latin plicare)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: verb-forming suffix

Put it together

Put it together: Com- ('together') plus plic- ('to fold') plus -ate gives 'to fold together.' Things folded into one another become tangled — and tangled things are harder to sort out.

Use the root in a new word: pliable

Use the root in a new word: pliable: The florist bent the pliable wire into a hoop — pliable means easy to fold or bend, from the same 'fold' root.

Root Check

Word Choice

Neutral / everyday

Complicate takes a situation, task, or process as its object — you complicate a plan, a case, or matters, never a person. The set phrase 'to complicate matters further' is a common way writers introduce yet another problem.
